title: Quantum Probability Current Guided Reduction of Coupling Control Degrees of Freedom for Excitation Transport
authors: Liuheng Cao, Lin Zhang, Junde Wu
abstract: Time-dependent coherent control can enhance excitation transport in open quantum networks, but independently controlling every inter-site coupling creates a control space of high dimension and leads to difficult optimization problems. We introduce an edge-ranking strategy based on the control-induced change in the gradient component of the time-integrated quantum probability current, which is obtained via a graph Hodge decomposition. When our strategy is applied to the seven-site Fenna-Matthews-Olson (FMO) model, the six-edge set retains $99.83\%$ of the enhancement achieved by full control, and the four-edge set retains $97.60\%$ while reducing the pulse fluence---used here as a proxy for control effort---by $41.55\%$ relative to full control. Dephasing scans and comparisons with random edge sets and random networks provide numerical support for the relevance and potential broader utility of the ranking. These results show that edge selection guided by the quantum probability current can substantially reduce the control space while preserving high transport performance with lower control effort.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of controlling excitation transport in complex quantum systems by reducing the number of necessary control parameters. The authors propose an edge-ranking method based on analyzing the quantum probability current's gradient component. This technique successfully identifies a small subset of couplings that preserves near-maximal transport efficiency while drastically lowering the required external control effort.
main_problem: The primary goal is to enhance excitation transport in open quantum networks while drastically reducing the high dimensionality of the required control space.
main_result: Edge selection guided by the quantum probability current can substantially reduce the control space, allowing for high transport performance (e.g., 97.60% retention) with significantly lower control effort (e.g., 41.55% reduction in fluence).
method: The authors introduce an edge-ranking strategy based on analyzing the change in the gradient component of the time-integrated quantum probability current, derived using graph Hodge decomposition.
model_or_system: The system is modeled after excitation transport in photosynthetic protein complexes, specifically using the seven-site Fenna-Matthews-Olson (FMO) model. Dynamics are governed by a Lindblad master equation incorporating coherent evolution and dissipation.
key_observables: Transport Efficiency ($\eta(T)$), Pulse Fluence (control effort proxy), Quantum Probability Current (gradient and cycle components).
important_parameters: The number of sites (e.g., seven for FMO), the degree of dephasing, and the specific set of controllable edges selected.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the sink and ground states are absorbing states, and the ranking criterion relies on the gradient component of the integrated quantum probability current.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the open network model structure (sites, ground, sink). Other figures likely show dephasing dependence and scatter plots comparing efficiency against the norms of the probability current components.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of high-dimensional control, introduces the quantum probability current and graph Hodge decomposition, develops the edge-ranking strategy based on the gradient component, and validates this strategy using the FMO model results.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, physically motivated diagnostic tool (the probability current gradient) to guide quantum control optimization, moving beyond brute-force optimization by identifying the most critical couplings.
